Fusion of powers is a feature of some parliamentary forms of government, where most, if not all, of the members of the executive must come from the legislature , and therefore the legislative and executive branches of government can be spoken of as being fused. [ 1 ] It is contrasted with the separation of powers [ 2 ] found in presidential , semi-presidential and dualistic parliamentary forms of government, where the membership of the legislative and executive powers cannot overlap. Fusion of powers exists in many, if not a majority of, parliamentary democracies, and does so by design. However, in all modern democratic polities the judiciary does not possess legislative or executive powers. [ a ]
